terms.definition: A statement of the terms on which the offeror is willing to be bound, made with the intention that it becomes binding as soon as it is accepted.
terms.examiner: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co: an offer can be made to the whole world (a unilateral offer).

terms.definition: An invitation to others to make an offer or to negotiate; it cannot be accepted to form a contract.
terms.examiner: Goods in a shop window (Fisher v Bell), goods on shelves (Pharmaceutical Society v Boots), advertisements (Partridge v Crittenden).

terms.definition: A final and unqualified agreement to all the terms of the offer.
terms.examiner: A counter-offer ends the original offer (Hyde v Wrench); a request for information does not (Stevenson v McLean). Acceptance must be communicated (Felthouse v Bindley).

terms.definition: Where post is a reasonable means of acceptance, acceptance is complete when the letter is posted, not when it arrives.
terms.examiner: Adams v Lindsell. It does not apply if the offer requires actual notice (Holwell Securities v Hughes). Instantaneous communication takes effect when received (Entores v Miles Far East).

terms.definition: Withdrawal of an offer. An offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance, but the revocation must be communicated to the offeree.
terms.examiner: Byrne v Van Tienhoven; communication can be by a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds). A unilateral offer cannot be revoked once performance has begun (Errington v Errington and Woods).

terms.definition: The parties must intend their agreement to be legally binding. Social and domestic agreements are presumed not to be; commercial agreements are presumed to be.
terms.examiner: Balfour v Balfour, rebutted in Merritt v Merritt; Edwards v Skyways, rebutted by an honour clause in Jones v Vernon's Pools. State the presumption, then say whether the facts rebut it.

terms.definition: What each party gives or promises in exchange for the other's promise.
terms.examiner: It must be sufficient but need not be adequate (Chappell v Nestlé, Thomas v Thomas); past consideration is not good consideration (Re McArdle; contrast Lampleigh v Braithwait); performing an existing duty is not enough (Stilk v Myrick) unless there is a practical benefit (Williams v Roffey).

terms.definition: Only the parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it.
terms.examiner: Tweddle v Atkinson; Dunlop v Selfridge. The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 s1 lets a third party enforce a term if the contract says so or the term purports to confer a benefit on them.
